questions.question: India and Pakistan became independent within a day of each other in August 1947. Why do they mark different dates?
options: Pakistan declared early, before the handover was legal
The two countries use different calendar systems
Mountbatten attended each ceremony, a day apart
Pakistan chose a date with religious significance
questions.answer: Mountbatten attended each ceremony, a day apart
questions.explanation: Louis Mountbatten, the last Viceroy, attended both transfers in person, Pakistan's in Karachi on 14 August and India's in Delhi at midnight on the 15th. The boundary itself had been drawn by Cyril Radcliffe, a lawyer who had never been to India, working in about five weeks. It was finalised on 12 August but not published until the 17th, so for days millions did not know which country they were in. Somewhere between 12 and 20 million people crossed the new borders.
questions.memory_hook: Mountbatten went to both ceremonies, so Pakistan's was 14 August in Karachi and India's 15 August in Delhi. The border was drawn in five weeks by a lawyer who had never visited India, and it was not published until the 17th, so for two days people did not know which country they lived in.

questions.question: The Battle of Waterloo in 1815 ended whose rule over much of Europe?
options: Maximilien Robespierre
Louis XIV
Napoleon Bonaparte
Frederick the Great
questions.explanation: The Battle of Waterloo (June 18, 1815) in present-day Belgium was Napoleon's final defeat. He was defeated by the Duke of Wellington's allied forces and Prussian troops. Napoleon abdicated four days later and was exiled to Saint Helena island in the South Atlantic, where he died in 1821. The battle permanently ended French domination of Europe and established the peace settlement of the Congress of Vienna.
questions.memory_hook: Waterloo 1815 = Napoleon's final defeat. He was exiled to Saint Helena in the South Atlantic — as far from Europe as possible. He died there 6 years later. The battle lasted one day and ended 20 years of Napoleonic wars. ABBA later immortalized the defeat in a song.
questions.canonicalNote: Waterloo and Napoleon are fixed and universally attested

questions.question: Jamestown was founded in 1607 as England's first lasting settlement in North America. What nearly ended it?
options: A fire set deliberately by a rival Dutch expedition
A hurricane that destroyed the settlement completely
A winter of starvation that killed most of the colonists
An epidemic brought over on the original three ships
questions.answer: A winter of starvation that killed most of the colonists
questions.explanation: The winter of 1609 to 1610 is called the Starving Time. Of roughly 500 people in James Fort at the start of it, about 61 were alive by spring, and archaeological work has confirmed survival cannibalism from cut marks on the skull of a fourteen-year-old girl the researchers call Jane. It was not only bad farming: a Powhatan siege cut the fort off from outside relief, and the site had been picked for defensibility on brackish marshland. Survivors had boarded ships to abandon it when a resupply fleet arrived.
questions.memory_hook: The Starving Time of 1609-10 left about 60 alive out of 300, and archaeologists have found cut marks on a fourteen-year-old girl's skull confirming cannibalism. The site was picked for defence, not farming, on brackish marsh. Survivors were literally sailing away when resupply arrived.

questions.question: Judo was created in 1882 by Jigoro Kano, drawing from older jujutsu schools. What did Kano deliberately remove?
options: Strikes and joint locks too dangerous to practise fully
Competition entirely, leaving only solo forms
All groundwork, keeping only standing throws
The ranking system, so nobody could claim seniority
questions.answer: Strikes and joint locks too dangerous to practise fully
questions.explanation: Kano stripped out the techniques that could not be trained at full intensity without injury, which let students practise randori, live sparring against a resisting opponent, rather than rehearsing set forms. The dangerous material was preserved in kata rather than discarded. That was the innovation, and it is why judo could be tested competitively and entered the Olympics at Tokyo in 1964. Kano also devised the coloured belt and dan grading system, which spread to virtually every other martial art.
questions.memory_hook: Kano removed what could not be practised at full speed safely, so students could spar live against real resistance instead of rehearsing forms. That is why judo could be competed at all. He also invented coloured belts and the black belt, which nearly every other martial art then copied.

questions.question: A volleyball dig keeps a spiked ball alive. What makes it so difficult?
options: It must be played with a closed fist to be legal
Only the libero is permitted to attempt one at all
The digger has to call it aloud before the ball lands
The ball can arrive at over 100 km/h from close range
questions.answer: The ball can arrive at over 100 km/h from close range
questions.explanation: Elite men's spikes have been measured above 130 km/h, hit downward from above net height a few metres away, so the defender has roughly two to three tenths of a second and is usually reacting before the ball is struck. Digging is about reading the hitter's shoulders and approach rather than watching the ball. The libero specialises in it, but any player may dig, and there is no requirement to use a fist or to call for it.
questions.memory_hook: Elite spikes come down at over 130 km/h from a few metres away, so you are reacting before contact and reading the hitter's shoulders rather than the ball. The libero specialises in digging but anyone can do it, with no fist rule and no calling for it.

questions.question: Toy Story (1995) was the first fully computer-animated feature. What limitation shaped how it looks?
options: Toys were chosen because plastic was easy to render
The film could not exceed forty minutes of footage
Every frame had to be drawn by hand and then scanned
Only three colours could be displayed at that time
questions.answer: Toys were chosen because plastic was easy to render
questions.explanation: In 1995 organic surfaces were beyond the hardware: skin, hair and cloth rendered so poorly that anything soft came out looking like plastic. Pixar leaned into that and built the story around objects the technology could actually do, and the team initially planned to keep humans out of frame entirely rather than animate them badly. Rendering ran up to 30 hours a frame across a farm of 117 Sun SPARCstation 20s, roughly 800,000 machine hours for 114,200 frames.
questions.memory_hook: 1995 hardware could not do skin, hair or cloth, but shiny plastic was easy, so Pixar built the story around toys. The humans in it still look bad. Some frames took 30 hours to render across 117 workstations. Disney expected a flop, which is why Pixar got left alone.

questions.question: The Eagles' Hotel California has been argued over for decades. What did Don Henley say the title track is actually about?
options: A coded account of a satanic church in Los Angeles
American excess and the underside of the music industry
A psychiatric hospital where a band member was treated
A real hotel in Baja California he had stayed in
questions.answer: American excess and the underside of the music industry
questions.explanation: Henley has repeatedly described it as a song about excess and disillusion in 1970s America, using a hotel as the metaphor, and has expressed irritation at the more elaborate theories. The Church of Satan reading, and the claim that a specific Mexican hotel inspired it, both persist regardless. The album took eight non-consecutive weeks at number one on the Billboard 200 across four separate stints in 1977, and the guitar duel between Don Felder and Joe Walsh is among the most analysed in rock.
questions.memory_hook: Henley says it is about American excess and the ugly side of the music business, with the hotel as metaphor, and he finds the other theories tiresome. The satanic church and the real-Mexican-hotel stories refuse to die anyway. Eight weeks at number one, and that Felder and Walsh guitar duel.

questions.question: Grant Wood's American Gothic (1930) is usually taken as satire of the rural Midwest. What did Wood say about that?
options: He said he had meant it as a joke on his own family
He accepted it but blamed the Art Institute's framing
He rejected it, meaning the rural values kindly
He never discussed the painting's meaning publicly
questions.answer: He rejected it, meaning the rural values kindly
questions.explanation: Wood denied the satirical reading for the rest of his life and said he had intended reassurance about rural American values at the start of the Depression. The models were his dentist B.H. McKeeby and his sister Nan, posed as a farmer and his daughter rather than as a couple, in front of a Carpenter Gothic farmhouse he had seen at Eldon, Iowa. It won a $300 prize at the Art Institute of Chicago in 1930 and made him famous immediately, and the ambiguity is exactly why viewers kept supplying their own story.
questions.memory_hook: The most parodied painting in America is one whose maker spent his life saying everyone had it backwards.

questions.question: Africa is the only continent with land in all four hemispheres. What line runs almost exactly through its middle?
options: The Tropic of Cancer, which bisects the continent
The equator, crossing seven African countries
The Prime Meridian, running down its eastern edge
The Arctic Circle, clipping the northern coast
questions.answer: The equator, crossing seven African countries
questions.explanation: The equator crosses Gabon, Congo, DR Congo, Uganda, Kenya, Somalia and Sao Tome and Principe, and the Prime Meridian passes through Ghana, Togo, Burkina Faso, Mali and Algeria. Their intersection at zero latitude and zero longitude sits in the Gulf of Guinea, off Ghana. That combination puts African land north, south, east and west of both lines, which no other continent manages.
questions.memory_hook: The equator crosses seven African countries and the Prime Meridian crosses five, and they meet in the Gulf of Guinea just off Ghana. That is why Africa has land in all four hemispheres, which no other continent manages.
questions.canonicalNote: atlas-level geography; the equator and prime meridian crossings are fixed

questions.question: A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the surface. What causes that?
options: Water magnifies whatever sits behind it
Water absorbs some colours, distorting the outline
Light changes speed entering water, so its path bends
The eye cannot focus on two distances at once
questions.answer: Light changes speed entering water, so its path bends
questions.explanation: Light travels slower in water than in air, and at an angled boundary the change in speed bends the path, which is refraction. Your brain assumes light travelled in a straight line, so it places the submerged part of the straw where it would have been if unbent. The same effect makes pools look shallower than they are, produces rainbows by splitting colours that bend by different amounts, and is what every lens exploits.
questions.memory_hook: Light slows down entering water, and at an angle that bends its path. Your brain assumes light came straight, so it draws the straw in the wrong place. Same reason pools look shallower than they are, and why rainbows work, since each colour bends by a slightly different amount.

questions.question: The Sea of Japan lies between Japan and the Korean Peninsula. By what name do South Korea and Japan disagree on what this body of water should be called?
options: Both agree it should be the Pacific Sea
Japan insists on calling it the Korea Sea
Korea calls it the East Sea; both names are used
The UN has ruled it must be called the Pacific Ocean
questions.answer: Korea calls it the East Sea; both names are used
questions.explanation: South Korea calls it the East Sea, Donghae; North Korea the East Sea of Korea; Japan the Sea of Japan. The dispute turns on how the name became standard: the International Hydrographic Organization adopted Sea of Japan in its 1929 reference work while Korea was under Japanese colonial rule and had no seat at the table, and Korea did not join the IHO until 1957. Seoul has campaigned for dual naming since 1997. The IHO rejected the change in 2012 and has since moved to a digital standard using numeric identifiers instead.
questions.memory_hook: Sea of Japan vs. East Sea: Japan and Korea have a naming dispute. Korea says 'Sea of Japan' was imposed during colonization (1910-1945). Now many international bodies use both names. Geography and history intertwined — even naming a sea is political.

questions.question: A mutation is a change in a DNA sequence. What makes most of them harmless?
options: Cells destroy any DNA strand that has been altered
Mutations only occur in cells about to die anyway
The second copy of each chromosome overrides it
Much of the genome does not code for any protein
questions.answer: Much of the genome does not code for any protein
questions.explanation: Only around 1 to 2% of human DNA codes for proteins, so a random change most often lands somewhere with no direct effect. The genetic code is also redundant, with several triplets specifying the same amino acid, so even a coding change frequently produces an identical protein. Cells additionally run repair machinery that catches most errors before they stick. Mutations that do matter are the raw material evolution works with.
questions.memory_hook: Only 1 to 2% of your DNA codes for proteins, so a random change usually lands somewhere inert. The code is also redundant, with several triplets meaning the same amino acid, so many coding changes still make the same protein. Repair machinery catches most of the rest.
questions.canonicalNote: textbook genetics; the ~1-2% coding figure is universally attested
